parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Remember there are seven SI base quantities in total, and three are already given. Think about what other fundamental things we measure that cannot be built from mass, length and time alone.
Hint 2: Think of one quantity linked to electricity and one linked to heat or to chemistry and light. Each has its own base unit such as ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a base quantity means**
Think of base quantities as the building blocks. Every other quantity in physics, like velocity, force or energy, can be made by combining them. There are exactly seven to learn.

Step 2: **Recall the full set of seven**
You already have mass ($\text{kg}$), length ($\text{m}$) and time ($\text{s}$). The other four are electric current ($\text{A}$), thermodynamic temperature ($\text{K}$), amount of substance ($\text{mol}$) and luminous intensity ($\text{cd}$). Any two of these earn the marks.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: The hook is in equilibrium, so forces up must balance forces down. Look at the diagram and ask yourself which part of the 150 N tension actually pulls upward to support the tyre.

Hint 2: Each side of the wire makes 17 degrees with the horizontal. Consider how to get the small vertical part of each 150 N force and why you must add the contributions from both left and right sides.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the balance at the hook**
The tyre pulls straight down with its weight $W$. The only things pulling up are the two halves of the wire. Because the rope and hook are negligible, $W$ must equal the total upward pull from the wire for equilibrium.

Step 2: **Resolve each tension vertically**
Each side has tension $T = 150\text{ N}$ at $17^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The upward component on one side is:
$$T_{v} = T \sin 17^{\circ}$$
There are two identical sides, so:
$$W = 2T \sin 17^{\circ} = 2 \times 150 \times \sin 17^{\circ}$$
$$W = 87.7\text{ N} \approx 88\text{ N}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start with stress. Think about how concentrated the 150 N pull is. A thinner wire feels a larger internal effect, so focus on force and cross-sectional area.
Hint 2: Check your area units before dividing. Convert $7.5\text{ mm}^2$ into $\text{m}^2$ using $1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}$, then divide the 150 N tension by that area.

Hint 3: Now move to strain. Remember Young modulus $E$ links how much stress you apply to how much fractional stretching you get, and the wire obeys Hooke's law so you can use $E = \text{stress} / \text{strain}$.
Hint 4: Rearrange to strain = stress / $E$ and substitute your stress value and $E = 2.1 \times 10^{11}\text{ Pa}$. Check that strain has no units.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Calculate stress - force per unit area**
Stress tells you the internal force per square metre inside the wire:
$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$$
Convert area:
$$A = 7.5\text{ mm}^2 = 7.5 \times (10^{-3}\text{ m})^2 = 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$$
Then:
$$\sigma = \frac{150}{7.5 \times 10^{-6}} = 2.0 \times 10^{7}\text{ Pa}$$

Step 2: **Calculate strain using Young modulus**
Young modulus is defined as:
$$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$$
So strain is:
$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E}$$
Substitute:
$$\varepsilon = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{7}}{2.1 \times 10^{11}} = 9.5 \times 10^{-5}$$
Strain is a ratio of lengths, so it has no unit. The very small value makes sense because steel is very stiff.
